blocks.text: Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Taymiyya (661-728 AH, years of the Muslim calendar) is remembered today as a renewer of the Hanbali school, one of the four Sunni schools of law. His own tradition tells a fuller story. A biographical dictionary, a travel diary, his own collected works, and the later verdicts of the Shafi'i school document it. The talent is conceded, in the words of his own contemporaries and students. His collected works teach where God is. The creed incidents repeatedly put him before councils of judges. The grave-visitation ruling sent him to his final prison. A proclamation was made in Damascus in 705, and in 707 in Cairo a creed from his own hand was produced against him. Later authorities of the Shafi'i school and one Hanbali of his own line also recorded verdicts against him.

blocks.text: Ibn Taymiyya was a leading Hanbali jurist of Damascus, a man of great standing who spoke on the sciences, and a man in whom the traveler found something wrong with his mind. The report of the sermon that follows is Ibn Batuta's own, from a Friday he says he attended in the congregational mosque.

blocks.text: Preaching on the descent of God, Ibn Taymiyya descended one step of the pulpit to illustrate the manner of the descent. When the Maliki jurist Ibn al-Zahra objected from the congregation, the crowd beat him with hands and sandals until his turban fell, before any judge acted. The Hanbali judge of Damascus then imprisoned the objector and had him disciplined. The Maliki and Shafi'i jurists carried the protest to Tankiz, the commander of the emirs. The report carries no date of its own.

blocks.text: The sermon Ibn Batuta heard does not stand alone. His collected works carry both the creed and the visitation ruling. Where God is, and what the verses that describe God's attributes mean, he answers in his own prose.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: People divided into four camps when the Jahmiyya emerged, an early group that denied that God is above His creation, and he names the position he counts his own. The Salaf, the earliest generations of Muslims, and the imams hold that God is above His heavens, upon His Throne, separate from His creation, on the authority of the Book and the Sunnah. That doctrine is what the later Shafi'i verdicts itemize under corporeality and direction.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The proofs he reaches for are two texts about heaven. The Prophet ﷺ asks a slave girl where God is, she answers that He is in heaven, and he accepts the answer as faith itself. Zaynab ﵍ boasts before the other wives that God married her from above His seven heavens. From the second report Ibn Taymiyya derives a consensus.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The Qur'an itself, on his reading, informs that God is in heaven. The verses that say He who is in heaven he takes as words naming where God is. He sets them beside the verses He is the God in heaven and on earth, and the Prophet's ﷺ description of himself as the trustworthy one of Him who is in heaven. He gathers what God and the Messenger say about where God is, and the texts he cites name heaven.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The old formula of the Salaf, pass the reports on as they came without asking how, was widely read among the kalam theologians as a refusal to say what the words mean. Ibn Taymiyya reads it the other way. The Salaf denied knowledge of the modality, and they did not deny the reality of the attribute. That is the reading at issue in Cairo in 707. A creed in his own handwriting was produced against him, denying that the establishment over the Throne, the istiwa of the Qur'anic verse, is according to its apparent sense.

blocks.text: A traveler who sets out to visit the graves of the prophets believes he is performing an act of obedience, and the act is not one. Seeking nearness to God through what is not obedience is disobedience, and the prohibition entails forbiddance. He notes that some later scholars permitted the travel, and the Arabic excerpt breaks off inside the name of the first of them. The next page completes the name, Abu Hamid, the author of the Ihya, followed by two more. He also answers the summary form of the charge himself.

blocks.text: The denial and the ruling sit together without contradiction, on his own terms. The ruling forbids the journey taken to visit, and the denial rejects the claim that he forbids the visit itself. Both texts are his, and the dossier Tankiz sent the sultan survives in the Rihla.

blocks.text: The dossier named the rulings as errors. The threefold divorce counted as one. The pilgrim who intends the visit of the grave does not shorten his prayer. The order that followed confined Ibn Taymiyya to the citadel of Damascus, where he remained until he died.

blocks.text: A muezzin called on the Prophet as his means to God, in lines he recited from the minaret before dawn. Ibn Shakir told the muezzin that he had committed associationism, the sin of calling on other than God. A crowd then moved to behead Ibn Shakir, and his Islam was renewed for him. Al-Hisni, transmitting the historian roughly a century after the events, says the beating was severe and remarks that the follower softened the record out of regard for his teacher.

blocks.text: The chronology that follows is Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani's. It opens in Damascus with the imprisonment of the hadith master al-Mizzi, whom Ibn Taymiyya went to the prison and brought out with his own hand.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The judge of Damascus took the matter to the citadel. Ibn Taymiyya quarreled with him in the presence of the governor's deputy. The deputy had it proclaimed that whoever spoke on the creed would be punished, to still the disturbance. The council of Rajab 705 followed. In Ramadan came the summons to Cairo.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Before the Maliki judge of Egypt the claim against him was read, and he would not answer it.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The Maliki judge stated the holding, that his unbelief was established and that he must be confined if not killed. A proclamation ran over Damascus that whoever held Ibn Taymiyya's creed had forfeited his blood and property. The Hanbalis of al-Salihiyya, a quarter of Damascus, were assembled to testify against themselves that they held the creed of al-Shafi'i. Two years later, in Cairo, a deposition was drawn against him and a creed in his own handwriting was produced.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The creed in his handwriting affirms that the Qur'an is neither letter nor sound. It affirms that the establishment over the Throne is not according to its apparent sense, and that the statement concerning descent is like the statement concerning establishment. It was the Ash'ari creed, the theology of the kalam school, and it marks how far the concession went. On the fifteenth of Rabi al-Awwal 707 the witnesses certified that he repented from whatever contradicted it, willingly by the record's own word. Later that same year the Sufis of Cairo complained to the citadel. They said he spoke against the masters of the path and taught that no aid is sought from the Prophet. He was sent back toward Syria.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Proceedings over the divorce ruling in Ramadan 719 tightened the ban on his legal opinions. Another council in Rajab 720 sent him to the citadel, and Ashura 721 brought release. The visitation ruling brought proceedings again in Shaban 726, the citadel again, and this time no release. He died there on the night of Monday, the twentieth of Dhu al-Qa'da 728. Safadi's couplet, which Ibn Hajar sets at the close of the chronology, was one Ibn Taymiyya himself often recited.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Eight poets are named, and the entry adds a great multitude beyond them. Ibn Hajar also transmits a letter on the mood of Egypt.

blocks.text: In the letter Ibn Hajar transmits, all of Egypt spoke against him, the judges, the shaykhs, the Sufis, the scholars, and the common people. The Hanafi judge stood excepted as his partisan and the Shafi'i as silent. Damascus differed. Its Hanafi judge Shams al-Din al-Hariri defended him and wrote a document in his praise.

blocks.text: The Verdicts of the Later School

blocks.text: The later Shafi'i authority Ibn Hajar al-Haytami of Mecca (d. 974 AH), a different Ibn Hajar from the author of al-Durar al-Kamina, itemized the contraventions in his collected verdicts. The list survives in relay and is quoted here as the relayers preserve it.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The items are the doctrine of the eternity of the world in kind and the affirmations of corporeality, direction, and transfer for God, claims that He has a body, occupies a place above, and moves. The list also holds the affirmation that God is the size of the Throne, neither smaller nor larger. The same authority's summary verdict survives in the edition of al-Subki's Shifa' al-Saqam, and the quotation names him al-Makki, which is the same Ibn Hajar al-Haytami.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Al-Hisni of Damascus, a century closer to the events than al-Haytami, wrote his book to answer the visitation rulings, and he writes as an open partisan of that cause. His verdict is his own position, not a finding the record establishes.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: He builds it from a run of Shafi'i authorities on the visitation, from al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib to al-Mahamili to al-Halimi.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, of Ibn Taymiyya's own school two generations later, is recorded by al-Hisni among those who believed him an unbeliever, and the report survives only in al-Hisni's relay. The entry continues on the following page.

blocks.text: There Ibn Rajab is reported excusing al-Subki, the Shafi'i imam cited in the verdict above, for declaring him an unbeliever. Against all of this stands the obituary of al-Dhahabi, his own student, which Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani transmits.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: Al-Dhahabi concedes the learning, the memory, the courage, and the devotion, and refuses him infallibility. He disagrees with him on fundamental and subsidiary questions. He names the sharpness in debate, the anger, and the harshness toward opponents as the traits that bred enmity toward him, and adds that his opponents' petulance kept him from being a point of consensus. He defends him from the charge of trifling with religion and of lone caprice in his rulings, and closes with days of severe illness and death in the citadel. The obituary is the assessment of a student who knew him, and the enmity it names is the same enmity the record shows reaching the rulers.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: What the Record Supports
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: He taught, in his own collected works, that God is above His heavens, upon His Throne, separate from creation and in heaven, and that the attribute is real with only the how unknown. He ruled, in the same collection, that travel to visit the graves of the prophets is disobedience. He was summoned before the judges of Egypt in 705, and it was proclaimed in Damascus that whoever held his creed forfeited blood and property. In 707 the creed from his own hand, denying the apparent sense, was produced against him in Cairo. He was imprisoned repeatedly across twenty-three years, the last confinement in 726 for the visitation ruling, and he died in the citadel in 728. The grammarian Abu Hayyan praised him in verse and then broke with him. The later authorities of the Shafi'i school itemized his contraventions and recorded verdicts up to declared unbelief, in relay, and a Hanbali of his own line is recorded, in a single relay, holding that view.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The record also carries its qualifications. The minbar report is a traveler's eyewitness account, undated in the text of the Rihla. The 707 document exists, and its witnesses certified a repentance the record itself calls voluntary, so the motive question stays open. Ibn Taymiyya himself denounced as slander the summary form of the visitation charge, and his own volume holds both the ruling and the denial. The proclamation of 705 was issued amid the war of the judges of Cairo. And al-Dhahabi's obituary is the counterweight, a student's defense that concedes the sharpness and rejects the charge of trifling with religion.
blocks.observation: Read in the full five-role council cycle; content traced to its quoted evidence and the council dispositions applied this run.

blocks.text: The record also shows Shaykh Nasr al-Manbiji inciting the ruler Baybars against him over the Ibn al-Arabi letter, and the judges of Cairo fighting their own war through his case. The councils that tried him were councils of his own tradition's judges, the confinement orders were the sultan's and the governor's, and the verdicts are the verdicts of the school's own later authorities. The career is documented by the people who wrote the history of the tradition he belonged to.
